AIcoach · UX exploration · 11 Nov 2026

15 design concepts for AIcoach

Concepts 01–10 are the first round. Concepts 11–15 are a second round made with the frontend-design method, and each one's notes include its design plan. Each concept draws the same app with the same example data: Rory's early-extension result, Nelly's "No verified fault found", and a rejected face-on clip. Every concept shows the landing page, upload (desktop and phone), the result page with drills and the AI coach chat, plus a sheet of the remaining pages. Use By concept to read one direction end to end, or By page to compare all of them on the same screen.

01

Clubhouse Editorial

One swing. One honest letter back.

Concept notes

Thesis: Every analysis comes back as a coach's letter about your swing, typeset like a long-form golf journal, and the letter says exactly how sure it is.

Rationale

This direction is for the 11-handicap who practises after work and has not had a lesson in years. He does not want a dashboard. He wants the feeling of a good coach sitting down and writing to him about one swing. A journal fits an honest coach because editorial form already has the habits honesty needs: captions say what a plate shows, footnotes say where a claim comes from, and corrections are printed openly. So the fault chain is a typeset sidebar with footnote evidence markers (¹ ² ³), every measurement sits next to its confidence band, and "Cannot analyse" and "No verified fault found" are set as headlines in the same voice as a verified fault, not as error states. The engraved line-art golfer, drawn as plates with oxblood hairlines (the address line and the 7% bracket), makes the key frames feel like evidence rather than decoration.

Palette

HexRole
#F3EEE3Paper: page background
#FBF8F1Sheet: letter sheet, inputs, chat letters
#E9E1D1Deep paper: sidebars (fault chain, filming checklist), honesty band
#ECE4D4Plate ground behind key frames and diagrams
#1B2420Ink: body text, engraving outlines
#1E4636Pine: brand, primary buttons, links, pose lines, confidence marks
#4E5D55Soft ink: secondary text, captions, datelines (≥4.5:1 on paper)
#7B2331Oxblood: the single accent. Faults, feel cue, measurement hairlines, drop caps, unverified labels, destructive actions
#C8BDA8Hairline rules

Typography

  • Fraunces (300–600, italic): display. Headlines ("Early extension."), plate captions, the feel-cue pull quote, link names in the fault chain.
  • Source Serif 4 (400/600, italic): long-form reading text. The explanation letter, chat replies, standfirsts.
  • Hanken Grotesk (400–700): quiet UI sans. Navigation, buttons, labels, datelines, measurements, confidence lines.

Signature moves

1. The result is a letter. Drop cap opening, a standfirst that states the measurement and threshold, and the feel cue set as an oxblood pull quote between hairlines. 2. Plates as evidence. Address and impact appear as captioned engraved plates (Plate I and Plate II). An oxblood address line runs up from the backside, and at impact a bracket marks the 7% shift (threshold 4%). The text refers back to the plates by name. 3. Fault chain with footnotes. Likely cause, then mechanism, then fault, typeset as a sidebar. Each link carries a footnote marker that resolves to its evidence and confidence band. 4. Confidence marks. Three small squares (■■■ / ■■□ / ■□□) sit beside the words "Confidence: high/medium/low" on every measurement, everywhere.

How the AI chat lives here

"Ask your coach" sits in the right margin column under the fault chain and reads as correspondence. Each message has a header ("FROM RORY · 18:42" or "YOUR COACH"). Coach replies are set on letter sheets and cite the same footnotes and plates as the article ("Plate II … 7% of your body height²"). A seal-and-tick line reads "Answers are based only on this analysis." The sample includes a grounded refusal ("Will this fix my slice?" → "I can't tell from this analysis…"). Suggested prompts are hairline pills. The compose box reads "Write to your coach about this analysis…" with the reminder "No new faults, numbers or drills." On the phone, the chat is a button below the summary.

Risks / trade-offs

  • Reading-heavy. The letter voice rewards a sit-down read. At the range, a player with 30 seconds needs the phone summary (headline, plates, feel cue, drill) to carry the moment. The full letter has to stay one tap away and never be the only path.
  • Line-art golfer fidelity. Engraved figures look calm, but the real key frames will be video stills. The production design has to let real frames sit inside the same plate frame and hairline system without clashing with the engraved style. Engraving may end up reserved for marketing and diagrams.
  • Editorial tone can read as old-fashioned or "premium club" to younger players. The restraint (one accent, no gold or crests) has to be held firmly so it reads as calm authority, not exclusivity.
02

Lab Instrument

A coach that shows its working.

Concept notes

Thesis: A coach that shows its working.

Rationale

AIcoach is built for the +2 to 15 handicap player who already distrusts swing apps that hand out graphs and verdicts with no reasons. This concept treats every result like a page from a measurement report. The 7% reading is plotted against the 4% threshold with an error bar, key frames are pose-skeleton plots with keypoint markers and coordinate ticks in body heights, and the fault chain is a schematic in which every block carries its evidence callout and confidence band. The honesty in the PRD (Cannot analyse, No verified fault found, Unverified, possible) is not hidden in empty states. Each one gets an instrument readout of its own, so "refuses to guess" is shown instead of claimed. Swiss discipline keeps a dense page readable: margin labels, one signal colour, hairline rules and no decoration that does not measure something.

Palette

HexRole
#EEF0F1Paper: cool light-grey page ground
#F8F9F9Sheet: plots, panels, cards
#111417Ink: text, rules, skeleton lines, primary buttons
#3E464D / #5C646BSecondary / tertiary ink (captions, units, mono metadata)
#E1E5E8 / #CDD3D7Graph-paper grid, minor and major (only under plots and measuring surfaces)
#D2D8DCGhost body capsules behind the skeleton
#E2471ASignal: measured value, error bar, confidence meter, the hip keypoint. The only colour
#B23A10Signal text on light (AA contrast)
#101316 / #FF7A4FConsole ground / signal on dark, used only in the AI chat

Typography

  • Inter Tight (400/500/600/700): display headlines (tight tracking, -0.02 to -0.03em), body copy, coach-voice explanation, feel cue.
  • JetBrains Mono (400/500/700): only for data. That means measurement IDs (M-01, F-IMP, R-EE, D-01), values, units, axis ticks, timestamps, the analysis log and the chat console. The wordmark sets "AI" in mono and "coach" in Inter Tight, which also stops "AI" reading as "Al".

Signature moves

1. Threshold ruler with error bar. Each measurement is a ruler: the fault threshold is a hard line, the zone above it is hatched, a possible fault has a dashed potential-threshold line, and the value is a diamond with an error bar. Confidence shows twice: as the width of the bar and as a 3-cell meter (■■■ conf HIGH). 2. Key frames as pose plots. Address and impact are drawn as skeletons with keypoint markers on graph paper, in body-height units. The impact plot overlays the dashed address pose and a dimension line (+0.070 BH) from the address hip line. 3. Fault chain as a schematic. Likely cause has a dashed border (inferred), mechanism a solid border (measured), fault a double border (verified). Each block has a leader line to an evidence tag carrying its ID, numbers and confidence band. 4. Citable IDs everywhere. Every number has an ID that the explanation, the chat and the analysis log refer back to.

How the AI chat lives here

"Query this analysis" is a dark terminal console pinned in the right rail of the result page; on a phone it is a bar at the bottom. Its header says Answers are based only on this analysis and lists the IDs it is allowed to cite (M-01…M-04, F-ADR, F-IMP, R-EE, D-01, X-01). Each coach reply shows the sources it used, puts inline citations such as [M-01] in the signal colour, and can embed a small copy of the cited measurement ruler. When a question falls outside the analysis ("Is my grip causing this?"), the reply says the analysis cannot answer it and is tagged outside this analysis. Below the console sits a note: the coach explains, the rule table decides.

Risks / trade-offs

  • Density can intimidate. A 15-handicap player at the range may find a lab report cold. The feel cue and the plain-language explanation have to stay large and come first, or the coach's warmth gets lost under the instrumentation.
  • Error bars need teaching. Few golfers read uncertainty intervals. The 3-cell meter and the HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW words carry the meaning on their own, but the landing page has to explain the convention once (it does, in the "Confidence band" specimen).
  • Precision theatre. Figures like ±0.6 % BH, 0.93 and frame numbers suggest more accuracy than a 2D-pose MVP may deliver. All values here are synthetic. The real build must show only uncertainty values that the pipeline actually computes.
03

Night Range

One swing under the floodlights. The frame tells the truth.

Concept notes

Thesis: One swing under the floodlights, and the frame tells the truth: the video is the page, and every finding is drawn onto it.

Rationale

AIcoach's player is Rory at the range after work in a Norwegian November: dark at 16:00, floodlights on, a phone propped on his bag. Night Range is set in that world. Near-black blue-green, floodlight cones, turf stripes, and one hot ball-tracer lime that marks only what matters: the swing path, the glowing hip line at impact, the measured link in the fault chain, and the primary action. An honest coach shows you the frame instead of a score. So every page puts a key frame or the live clip at full size, with the result laid over it as a broadcast-style HUD (address line dashed, impact hip line glowing, "7%" printed next to the gap) rather than in cards. Confidence is drawn as signal bars on every measurement. Amber (sodium light) is kept for caution: Cannot analyse, possible, unverified, low confidence, and the medical notice.

Palette

HexRole
#060C0BNight: page background
#0B1614Surface: coach dock, panels
#12211ERaised: inputs, user chat bubbles
#223630 / #2F4A42Hairlines, empty confidence bars
#EAF2EEPrimary text (≈17:1 on night)
#A6BCB3Secondary text (≈9:1)
#7A928ATertiary/meta text (≈5:1)
#C6FF3DTracer lime: swing path, hip line at impact, measured values, primary buttons (text #08110A on it)
#FFB547Sodium amber: Cannot analyse, possible fault, unverified observation, low confidence, warnings
#FFF2D2Floodlight: lamp heads and light cones only (low-opacity gradients)

Typography

  • Barlow Condensed 700/800: display, uppercase headlines, fault names, overlay readouts ("EARLY EXTENSION", "7%").
  • Barlow 400–700: UI and body copy, chat, explanations.
  • IBM Plex Mono 400/500: timecodes, frame numbers, fps, thresholds and measurement units only (data, not decoration).

Signature moves

1. The tracer. One lime line per screen: ball flight in the hero, the playhead and hip-movement curve in the scrubber, the glowing hip line at impact, the solid "measured" link in the fault chain. The "likely cause" link is dashed, because it is inferred. 2. The scrubbable swing timeline. Under the result video: a filmstrip of the swing window (address, top, impact), with the hip-movement curve crossing the dashed 4% threshold exactly at the IMPACT marker. Playhead, frame step and ¼ speed controls. 3. Overlays, not cards. Verdict, confidence and measurement sit on the frame, with a leader line to the gap between the address line and the impact hip line. A ghost of the address pose sits under the impact pose.

The AI coach

A compact dark dock pinned to the right of the result, like a coach standing beside the bay. The first line says "Answers are based only on this analysis. No new faults, numbers or drills." Answers quote the analysis's own numbers and confidence, and carry lime reference chips (e.g. "Impact frame 00:01.42", "Wall drill") that move the scrubber or scroll to that part of the page. The sample includes a refusal ("I can't tell from this analysis — it doesn't measure grip … confirm with a coach") to show the grounding. Below the chat: suggested prompts and a pinned input. On phones the dock becomes a bottom sheet that peeks over the result.

Risks / trade-offs

  • Dark and moody can turn murky. Silhouette figures on a dark scene are low-contrast by design. Text contrast is checked, but key frames need real video plus a light scrim behind the overlays, or the HUD gets lost on bright clips (daylight ranges, white nets).
  • Real clips aren't composed like the drawings. The HUD layout assumes a predictable DTL framing. Badly framed clips that still pass analysis need a fallback that moves the readouts off the video, below the frame.
  • Cinematic can feel like a sports-broadcast brand. The condensed caps and lime accent must stay functional (only measured/verified things glow), or the honesty message turns into hype.
04

Coach's Notebook

Your swing, printed out and marked up by a coach: the app measures in white, the coach writes in red.

Concept notes

Thesis: Your swing, printed out and marked up by a coach. The app measures in clean white lines, and the coach writes over them in red marker.

Rationale

AIcoach is for the 2–15 handicap golfer who hasn't had a lesson in years and practises alone at the range. What they miss is not data. They miss a person who looks at their swing and says "there, that's it." This concept puts the product in that person's notebook: key frames printed and taped to grid paper, a red circle round the hips, a hand-written "hips →", the feel cue on a sticky note, the drill on an index card. Honesty comes from the material itself. The white lines are the app's measurements, the red marks are the coach's interpretation, and every page keeps those two layers visibly apart, so the player can always tell what was measured from what was inferred. The hand-made feel makes "Cannot analyse" and "No verified fault found" read as a coach's candid note, not an error screen. The page structure stays strict (one column of verdict, then evidence, then practice), so it reads as warm without getting messy.

Palette

HexRole
#F7F2E6Notebook paper (page ground)
#DCE5E8Grid rule lines (24 px squares)
#E5A99EPaper margin line
#1E2833Ink: text, primary buttons, sketch strokes
#545A62Pencil: secondary text, measurements context
#C8402ACoach's red marker: fault, annotations, rejection, destructive actions
#2F7A4DGreen: verified, confidence high, reps, ticks
#94550CAmber: confidence medium, possible fault, inferred links
#F8E07ASticky note (feel cue)
#FFFDF8 / #C6D9E5 / #E7A196Index card, blue card rules, red header rule
#2A4A9ABlue ballpoint: player's chat messages, links to the filming guide
#E2D3A6Masking tape
#CED7D1 / #7C9768 / #252E2AKey-frame photo: sky, range grass, golfer silhouette

Typography (Google Fonts)

  • Literata (400, 600, 700, italic 400). The voice for all content: headings, verdicts, evidence, explanation, UI. A sturdy book face that stays readable at 13 px on a phone in daylight.
  • Caveat (500, 700). Used only for the coach's hand: annotations on key frames, margin notes, the feel-cue sticky note and labels on sketches. It is never used for body text, numbers the player must rely on, or controls.

Signature moves

1. Printed key frames with two layers of ink. Address and impact appear as taped photo prints. The app's crisp white pose lines and the dashed "hip line at address" sit on the photo, and the coach's red circle, "hips →" and "7% of body height" are drawn on top in marker. 2. Paper objects as the information architecture. The verdict is an index card, the feel cue a sticky note, the drill and mobility exercise taped index cards with reps in green, the possible fault a dashed amber slip, the unverified observation a dashed scrap stamped "Unverified — confirm with a coach". 3. Hand-drawn rulers for thresholds. The measurement is a pencil ruler with the 4% fault threshold dashed and "you: 7%" in marker. Loss of posture gets the same ruler with the 5° potential and 9° fault lines. 4. Confidence as filled marker dots (●●● high, ●●○ medium, ●○○ low), always paired with the word, on every measurement and every chain link.

How the AI chat lives here

The chat feels like texting your coach. It is a taped sheet beside the result, titled "Ask your coach" and tied to "this result: Early extension · 11 Nov". Rory's messages are blue-ink bubbles. The coach's replies are paper bubbles and can include a small pencil sketch: the address and impact stick figures with the hip line and "+7%". A green-ticked note at the top says "Answers are based only on this analysis. No new faults, numbers or drills." The sample thread shows grounding at work. One reply quotes the 7% and the impact frame, one reuses the wall-drill text for a net, and one declines to talk about grip, a red margin note reading "won't guess". Suggested prompts are hand-cut paper chips. On mobile the chat opens from a full-width "Ask your coach about this" bar under the verdict.

Risks / trade-offs

  • Charm can read as amateur. The hand-drawn layer has to stay disciplined (Caveat for annotations only, strict grid, real type hierarchy). If Caveat spreads into body text or controls, the product looks like a hobby project and loses the trust the honesty pitch depends on.
  • Wobbly strokes cost implementation effort. Production needs a small SVG "rough" helper (seeded jitter) for boxes, circles and arrows, plus real-time overlay of the coach marks on frames whose geometry comes from the pose data. That is more work than CSS borders.
  • Density on phones. Taped cards, rotation and shadows eat width at 390 px. On mobile the rotations and tape should be toned down (the phone frames already flatten them), or the result will feel cramped at the range.
05

Scorecard Brutalist

Every swing gets one honest scorecard: ruled cells, fixed rows, and a red circle only where the rule table says so.

Concept notes

Thesis: Every swing gets one honest scorecard: ruled cells, a fixed set of rows, and a red pencil circle only where the rule table says so.

Rationale

AIcoach is for +2 to 15 handicap golfers who already fill in a scorecard every round, so the scorecard is a form they read without being taught. A card has a structure that cannot bend: the same three rows (early extension, loss of posture, over the top) and the same columns (measurement, threshold, confidence, evidence, mark) appear on every result. A fault cannot be slipped in and a doubt cannot be hidden. Empty cells, dashes and "no score" are shown as plainly as a verified fault, which is the product's honesty made visible: "Cannot analyse" is a card with nothing scored and a red line through it, and "No verified fault found" is three dashes. Paper, black rules and one scorer's red give a raw, high-contrast surface that still reads on a phone in daylight at the range. The heavy grotesk numerals make the one number that matters (7% against a 4% threshold) the loudest thing on the page.

Palette

HexRole
#F4F1EAPaper: every page background and cell fill
#111111Ink: rules, borders, header bars, body text, filled confidence cell
#D2231EScorecard red: the scorer's circle (verified), red body lines on key frames, rejection headline, warnings, destructive actions
#66645EPencil grey: thresholds, secondary notes, the address reference line, the player's typed questions in the chat
#CBC7BDFaint rule (a lighter pencil): ruled lines in the notes section only

Typography (Google Fonts)

  • Archivo Black: display voice and big numerals (7%, EARLY EXTENSION, CANNOT ANALYSE, 3 × 10).
  • Archivo 400/600/700/800: tiny tracked caps cell labels, controls, body copy, the coach's answers.
  • Courier Prime 400/700: typewriter text for data only: measurements, timestamps, file metadata, evidence lines, the player's own notes.

Signature moves

1. Scorer's marks as the status system. Circled in red = verified fault, boxed = possible fault, dash = not found. A legend under each card explains it, the same way a golf scorecard marks birdies and bogeys. 2. The confidence band as three cells, H M L. One is filled black. It sits in its own column on every row and on every link of the fault chain. 3. The page is a card. The nav is the card's header row. Player, handicap, club, date and frame rate are filled-in header fields. The fault chain is a table with row headers (link, status, evidence, key frame, confidence). Drill and mobility are "next session" cells with reps set like a score (3 × 10). 4. Pose skeleton key frames. Keypoints and bones, like the pose model's output. A dashed pencil line marks the hip at address and a red line marks the hip at impact, with the 7% gap shown with arrows.

How the AI chat lives here

The chat is the notes section at the bottom of the card: ruled lines with a red margin, speaker tags in the margin column (RORY / COACH). The player's questions are in pencil-grey typewriter text and the coach's answers in ink. The header bar reads "Answers are based only on this analysis". Under each answer, a "Based on" row of small cells names the exact parts of the card it used (hips toward the ball 7% · high, impact frame 1.79 s, posture angle 6°, wall drill). This makes the grounding something the player can check. One sample exchange shows the coach declining a question the card cannot answer ("This analysis does not look at your grip…"). Suggested prompts sit as outlined cells above a ruled input with an ASK cell.

Risks / trade-offs

  • Density and severity. A brutalist grid can feel like a form or a tax return. A golfer looking for warmth or motivation may find it cold, and the friendlier coach voice has to come entirely from the copy and the feel cue.
  • Thick rules and small caps labels. The 12px tracked labels and mono data are at the edge of what reads well outdoors on a phone. The mobile version needs larger labels and fewer columns than this sketch shows.
  • The metaphor depends on golf literacy. Circled/boxed marks only feel natural to players who keep score. The legend is needed, and the "possible = boxed" mark could be read as a bogey (a bad score) rather than "watch this".
06

The Coach Talks

One conversation per swing: the coach speaks in plain language, and every number it says is pinned to evidence.

Concept notes

Thesis: The whole app is one conversation per swing. The coach asks for the clip, watches it and answers in plain language. Every number it says is pinned to evidence you can check.

Rationale

This is for Rory: an 11-handicap who has not had a lesson in three years. He wants to be told what is wrong, not handed a dashboard. A real lesson is a conversation. The coach asks you to hit one, watches, says what it saw and gives you one thing to work on. So that is the structure here: upload, analysis progress and result all arrive as messages in one thread. The honesty is in the typography. The coach speaks in a warm serif, and anything measured is set in mono and teal with a numbered pin. Every pin shows up in a sticky Evidence panel with its key frame, value and confidence band. A sentence without a pin is explanation, never measurement, and the reader can see that at a glance. Faults and drills stay easy to scan because the coach does not deliver them as prose. They arrive as structured cards inside the thread (verdict, fault chain, practice, other checks), and a "Jump to" chip bar at the top of the thread indexes them.

Palette

HexRole
#F4EFE6Paper: page ground, the conversation surface
#EBE3D5Paper 2: left rail, disabled composer, quiet bands
#FFFCF6Card: verdict, chain and practice cards, inputs
#25201BInk: text, player bubbles, primary dark
#62584DInk 2: secondary text
#A4462AClay: the coach's colour (mark, name, feel-cue quotes, drill names, CTA)
#1E5368Evidence teal: measured values, pins, grounding note
#E2ECECEvidence tint: pins referenced by the latest answer
#2D6A4A / #8C5D0F / #8E3F33Confidence high / medium / low (always with the word and 3 bars)
#36312B + #8ED3E6Key-frame ground + body lines drawn on the golfer

Typography

  • Newsreader (400/500/600, italic): the coach's voice. Coach messages, headlines, the coach's name, the feel cue in italic.
  • Figtree (400–700): interface, player messages, card titles, labels.
  • IBM Plex Mono (500/600): measured evidence only (values, thresholds, swing-event times, step logs). It is used for measurement, not decoration.

Signature moves

1. Two voices, one rule. The coach writes in serif. Every measured number is mono and teal with a superscript pin [3], which matches a pin in the Evidence panel. The grounded chat answer ends with a "Based on: [3] hip movement · [2] impact frame" footnote. 2. Persistent Evidence panel. It stays beside the thread while you scroll: key frames 1–2, measurements 3–6 and clip checks. Pins the coach just cited are lit up. During analysis the pins fill in live. On the phone the panel becomes a pull-up evidence tray. 3. Dashed means inferred. The likely-cause link, the unverified observation and placeholders use dashed outlines. Anything measured gets a solid outline. 4. Upload is a message. The filming checklist is the coach's message, the composer turns into the drop zone, and progress streams in as a step log.

How the AI chat lives here

The chat is the product, not a widget added to a result page. Each swing has its own conversation, and that conversation is scoped to that swing's analysis. Under the composer, a lock note says "Answers are based only on this analysis — no new faults, numbers or drills." Suggested-prompt chips sit above the input. The landing page shows the grounding with a refusal ("I didn't measure your grip in this clip, so I can't tell you"). Nelly's no-fault thread shows the coach declining to invent a drill.

Risks / trade-offs

  • Chat as the frame can feel slow to someone who only wants the verdict. The "Jump to" chips and the structured cards keep it scannable, but returning users may still want a compact summary view.
  • The three-column desktop layout (rail, thread, evidence) is dense at 1280 px. On narrow laptops the evidence panel probably needs to collapse into a drawer.
  • A coach persona with a voice risks implying a human coach or more authority than the rule table has. The pins, confidence bands and dashed "inferred" language carry that honesty, so copy has to stay disciplined.
07

Yardage Book

Every fault has a route.

Concept notes

Thesis: every fault has a route. AIcoach surveys one swing the way a yardage book surveys a hole, and draws the route from likely cause to fault, marking what it measured, what it only infers and what it could not see.

Rationale

This is for the 2 to 15 handicap who already carries a yardage book or a rangefinder and trusts numbers they can check against the ground. A survey map is the most honest picture we have: it separates measured from inferred, it has a legend, and it leaves blank what nobody surveyed. That maps straight onto the product's edge. Confidence bands use map-line conventions (solid, dashed, dotted), "Cannot analyse" is an unsurveyed plot, and "No verified fault found" is a map with no route drawn. The user journey is played as a hole: tee (film), fairway (upload), green (result), next tee (practise). This journey strip runs at the top of every signed-in page. The look is outdoorsy and crafted but precise, so it reads like a tool a golfer can trust rather than a gamified app.

Palette

HexRole
#F2ECDFPaper: page background, the yardage-book page
#E9E1CEPanel paper: side panels, feel-cue box, action box
#22291FSurvey ink: text, route lines, primary buttons, caption strips
#4D5343Secondary ink: meta text, captions (5.9:1 on paper)
#5B7849Fairway: tee boxes, completed steps, check marks
#CCD6B2Light fairway: fairway fill, key-frame ground
#A9BF88Putting green: green, fault waypoint (3)
#DCC797Sand: bunkers, the "possible" zone on rulers
#A27F56Contour brown: contour lines, hatching on figures
#B23A2BCartographic red: annotations only (body lines, thresholds, swing arc, "Verified" stamp, leaders, current step, destructive actions)
#6E8E9EWater: notebook ruling in Caddie notes

Typography

  • Saira Condensed (500–800): display headlines, labels, map legends, numbers, buttons. It is condensed and technical, like the lettering on a survey sheet.
  • Source Serif 4 (400, 600, italic): body copy, coach explanation, feel cue (italic), chat answers. It is the human coach voice next to the surveyor's labels.

Signature moves

1. Contour hero generated from a swing arc. The landing hero is a marching-squares contour field computed from the distance to a down-the-line club path. The red arc carries survey triangles at takeaway, top, address/impact and finish, with a map legend and scale bar. 2. Fault chain as a route on a hole map. Waypoint 1 (likely cause, tee), 2 (mechanism, landing area) and 3 (fault, pin) each have an evidence callout on a red leader. The cause leg is dashed (medium, inferred). The measured leg is solid (high). Yardage plates on the route show 31° and 7%. 3. Map-legend confidence. Solid, dashed and dotted lines mean high, medium and low everywhere: tags, routes, borders (a possible fault has a dashed frame, an unverified observation a dotted one) and the analysing progress route. 4. Neatline sheet frame with graticule letters and numbers around every page, so each screen is a map sheet.

How the AI chat lives here

The chat is Caddie notes: a ruled notebook page with a binding margin, docked beside the result on desktop and a dark bar at the bottom of the phone result. A boxed note in its header says "Answers are based only on this analysis." Answers are tied to the evidence: each one ends with reference tags ("Impact key frame", "Waypoint 2 · 7%", "Wall drill") that point back to parts of the page. The sample also shows a refusal: asked for clubhead speed, the caddie says the analysis does not measure it and will not guess. Suggested prompts sit at the bottom as "Ask next" chips.

Risks / trade-offs

  • The map metaphor needs a legend, and some users won't read one. Dashed for medium is learned, not obvious, so the confidence words must always sit next to the line (they do in this concept). Line style alone is never enough.
  • Contours, hatching and stipple are dense. On a phone in sunlight at the range they can turn into noise, so the mobile screens deliberately drop texture and keep only the journey strip and line conventions.
  • The landing scroll is long (~4000 px). The Rule table and Honesty sections could be merged if the page needs to be shorter.
08

Broadcast Telestrator

Your swing gets the replay-analysis segment: marker on the hips, on-air stats, and an analyst who tells you how sure he is.

Concept notes

Thesis: Your swing gets the replay-analysis segment: frozen key frames, marker strokes on the hips, on-air stat graphics, and an analyst who tells you how sure he is.

Rationale

Built for Rory: an 11-handicapper who watches golf on TV and already knows the format: freeze the replay, circle the hips, draw the line the player left. AIcoach's core move is the same as that segment. It contrasts feel with what the frame shows, so the result page is staged as one: hero replay with telestration, a lower third naming the verified fault, then the fault chain run as a sequence of on-air graphics (likely cause → mechanism → fault), each carrying its evidence and confidence meter. The broadcast grammar is also a strong honesty tool. A confidence meter sits in every graphic the way a stat source line does on TV, so it is never hidden. Telestration is reserved for measured evidence. An unverified observation gets a dashed white outline instead, and a rejection shows "NO REPLAY" and does not draw on the frame. The energy keeps a range session moving; the plain-language copy and big slanted type stay readable on a phone in daylight.

Palette

HexRole
#081226Deep navy: studio background, ink on light plates
#0E1C3APanel navy: graphics, cards
#15274DRaised navy: active rows, feel-cue strap
#2A3F70Rule lines, frame borders
#FFFFFFLower-third plates, headlines
#D3DCEE / #A7B4D1Body text / secondary text on navy
#FF5B1FSignal orange: telestrator marker, REPLAY bug, drill, primary CTA (navy text on it)
#17C2AEConfidence teal: confidence meters, "VERIFIED", mobility, grounding note
#4A67A6 / #334C80Golfer figure (near/far limbs) in replay frames

Typography (Google Fonts)

  • Barlow Condensed: italic 800/900 for display, lower thirds, bugs, stat numerals; upright 700 for tickers and timecodes.
  • Barlow: 400/500/600/700 for body copy, explanations, chat, form fields.

Signature moves

1. Telestrator strokes: thick, freehand signal-orange marker lines drawn over the replay frames: the address hip line, a loop around the hips, and an arrow for the 7% shift. A translucent ghost of the address pose sits under the impact frame. 2. "REPLAY · IMPACT" bug plus timecode on every key frame, and lower-third plates ("EARLY EXTENSION" | "VERIFIED") with a confidence strap underneath. 3. Slanted confidence meter: three parallelogram bars with the word HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW. It appears on every measurement, link and fault. 4. The fault chain as numbered on-air graphics (1/3, 2/3, 3/3) joined by chevrons. "Likely cause" gets a dashed strap because it is not measured directly.

How the AI chat lives here

"Ask the analyst" is a studio Q&A desk in the result page's right column. Each question carries a white "RORY" name plate, and each answer an orange "ANALYST" plate. A lock note under the header states "Answers are based only on this analysis." An "On the desk" row lists the facts the analyst may use. Answers cite their evidence inline, for example a thumbnail of the telestrated impact frame and "Cited: 7% of body height (confidence: high)", and they link to the drill. An out-of-scope question ("Is my grip causing this?") gets an honest refusal tagged "Outside this analysis — not answered". Suggested prompts sit as chips above the input. On mobile, the desk collapses to a sticky bottom bar.

Risks / trade-offs

  • Broadcast energy can drift into "sports entertainment" and undercut the calm, trustworthy coach. The dense slanted plates need restraint in implementation, keeping one hero graphic per screen.
  • Telestration is drawn per fault. The production app would need overlay geometry generated from pose data, not hand-drawn art. The freehand look must be simulated reliably, for example as jittered SVG paths.
  • Dark navy with condensed italic caps is less legible in bright range sunlight than a light theme. Body copy stays in upright Barlow at 15px or larger, but a light "day mode" may be needed.
09

Cairn

A calm coach in one hand: your answer built one stone at a time, cause at the base, fault on top.

Concept notes

Thesis: A calm coach in one hand. It builds your answer one stone at a time, with the cause at the base and the fault on top, and it never stacks a stone it cannot balance.

Rationale

Cairn is for Rory at the range after work: phone in one hand, club in the other, a few minutes between balls. The phone is the main design surface. Each screen holds one thing (fault → why → what to practise → ask the coach), and every action sits in the bottom third within thumb reach. The cairn fits an honest coach because it is literal about evidence: a stone is only placed when the one beneath it holds, so the fault chain reads from the ground up (restricted hip rotation → hips move toward the ball → early extension). The same image covers the honest outcomes. "Cannot analyse" shows the stones lying unstacked on the ground. "No verified fault found" shows one flat, settled stone. An unverified observation is drawn as a dashed outline stone. Warm oat and stone neutrals, a single deep moss accent and a soft serif are meant to lower the player's shoulders instead of grading him. It should not feel bland, because the cairn appears on every surface.

Palette

HexRole
#F2EDE3Oat: page ground
#FBF8F2Linen: cards, sheets, inputs
#DDD5C6Stone: neutral pebbles, inactive track
#C9BFAEStone dark: dashed outlines, dividers on linen
#E3DBCCHairline
#E4E9DCSage light: feel cue, mobility card, chips
#C8D3BESage mid: medium-confidence stone fill
#A8B79FSage: leaders, secondary pebbles
#3E5638Moss: the one accent; primary buttons, high-confidence stones, body lines on key frames
#2A2925Ink: text, phone bezel, destructive confirm
#5C584FInk secondary: supporting text (≥4.5:1 on oat)
#8C8272Figure: golfer silhouette in key frames

Typography

  • Newsreader (400/500/600, italic): headlines, fault names, the feel cue (italic), dose numerals ("3 × 10").
  • Nunito Sans (400/600/700/800): all UI, body, labels, confidence badges. Body text is 15–16 px on the phone, and the smallest size is 12 px.

Signature move: the cairn

  • Fault chain = cairn. Stones are stacked with the cause at the bottom. Each stone has a fine leader line to its evidence and confidence.
  • Confidence = stone weight. High is a solid moss stone, medium is a sage-filled stone with a moss rim, and low is a dashed outline. The text label ("confidence: medium") is always shown as well, so colour is never the only signal.
  • Analysing builds the cairn. Pose, swing events, measurements, rule table and explanation each place a stone. The stone being placed hovers over a soft shadow, and the next one is a ghost outline.
  • The stepper is pebbles. Fault · Why · Practise · Ask: finished steps settle to sage, the current step is solid moss, and upcoming steps are dashed.
  • The logo is a three-stone cairn. The grounded-chat note reuses it as a tiny cairn icon.

How the AI chat lives here

The chat is the fourth and last step of the stepper: Ask. On the phone it opens as a bottom sheet over the dimmed result. A small cairn icon sits next to "Answers are based only on this analysis." Each coach answer ends with a "From:" line that names its sources (impact key frame, hip measurement, wall drill) and shows a thumbnail of the frame. Three suggested questions are shown as full-width chips, so there is no blank-page problem. On desktop the sheet docks under the practice cards as a panel, with the same note and chips. The chat comes after the player has seen the evidence, so it adds to the result and never replaces it.

Risks / trade-offs

  • Calm can read as low-energy. Competitive low handicappers may want more data density. The desktop adaptation stays deliberately sparse, so power users may find it slow.
  • The cairn metaphor has to be learned. Solid, half-tone and outline stones only work with the text labels next to them. If those labels are dropped to save space, the encoding fails. A one-time legend (as on the landing page) is needed.
  • Progressive disclosure hides things. "Possible fault" and "Over the top: not found" sit one step deeper ("Also checked"). Honest, but a player who stops at the first screen may miss them. The "Also checked: 2 more" link has to stay visible.
10

Kinetic Poster

Your swing as a poster: the stroboscopic arc, feel vs real, and the 7% shift as one bold arrow.

Concept notes

Thesis: The swing becomes a poster. A stroboscopic arc and two overlaid silhouettes show at a glance what you felt and what the video measured.

Rationale

This is for the 11-handicap who practises at the range after work. He doesn't want to read graphs. He wants to see the fault the way a coach would draw it on a whiteboard, only bolder. Geometric modernism suits an honest coach because it can only state what it can draw exactly. The address ghost is an outline, the impact body is solid, and the 7% hip shift is one bold arrow drawn to the figure's real scale. Nothing is airbrushed or implied. The confidence system is equally literal: a filled circle means high, a half circle means medium and an outline means low, so honesty is part of the graphics and not small print. Big expressive type gives the verdict ("EARLY EXTENSION", "CANNOT ANALYSE", "No verified fault found.") the weight of a headline. The working parts (upload, checklist, chat) stay crisp and quiet so the app remains usable on a phone at the range.

Palette

HexRole
#F3EFE6Paper: page ground
#E9E3D5Paper 2: quiet surfaces, mobility block, toggles
#15171EInk: type, rules, buttons, dark bands (honesty, analysing, key frames on #1C1F29)
#2343D8Cobalt: measured mechanism, address ghost, chat header, checklist, progress done
#EE4B2BVermilion: the fault, impact silhouette, primary "Analyse swing", rejection
#FFC531Yellow: the poster disc behind the golfer, suggested-prompt chips, "possible" badge
#C8D0F5Cobalt light: unverified observations, captions on cobalt

Typography

  • Unbounded (600/800/900, tracking -0.03em): display headlines, verdicts, measurements ("7%"), section titles.
  • Instrument Sans (400/500/600/700): body text, UI, labels, chat, data captions.

Signature moves

1. Stroboscopic swing arc. A fan of club-shaft lines around the hand path is drawn like a chronophotograph, with faded body exposures (half-way back, top, address) behind a solid impact figure. The same arc drives the logo mark, the dropzone and the analysing progress, which fills five segments (pose → swing events → measurements → rule table → explanation) along the swing arc. 2. Ghost vs solid overlay. The address body is an outline and the impact body is solid. A dashed backside line and a solid backside line sit side by side, with a bold arrow and a giant "7%" between them. The hip shift is drawn at the figure's true scale (7% of figure height). 3. Confidence glyphs. Filled, half and outline circles are used everywhere: results, the fault chain, the library and the chat source chips. 4. Colour-field fault blocks. Each of the three faults is a flat colour block with one quarter-circle corner.

How the AI chat lives here

On desktop the chat is a crisp white panel next to the result. On mobile it is a cobalt bar pinned to the bottom of the screen. Its header is cobalt with a small swing-arc mark, and directly under it a paper band states "Answers are based only on this analysis. It will not add faults, numbers or drills." Each coach answer is marked by a cobalt dot and line and ends with outlined source chips that point back into the result ("Impact key frame", "Hips 7% · high", "Wall drill", "Fault chain · likely cause"). This makes grounding visible. When asked, the coach also says what it is not sure about (restricted hip rotation is a likely cause, medium confidence). Suggested prompts are yellow pills. On the no-fault page, an unverified observation sends the player to the chat to ask what it is based on.

Risks / trade-offs

  • Unbounded is very wide. Long fault names and translated copy will need smaller sizes or more line breaks. Mobile headlines are capped at about 36px and use two lines.
  • Poster energy versus calm reading. The overlapping type and arc in the hero, and the dense chronophotograph, can feel busy. Keep the stroboscope to hero and result moments only, never in forms.
  • Contrast limits on vermilion. White text on vermilion only passes at large sizes, so small text on vermilion is always ink. Yellow is never used for text on paper.
11

Riso Zine

Your swing as a two-ink practice zine: halftone key frames, cut-out drill cards, and confidence printed as ink coverage.

Concept notes

Thesis: Every result is a small two-ink practice zine about one swing. How sure the coach is shows as how much ink it prints.

Rationale

This is for the club golfer, +2 to 15 handicap, who already trusts the photocopied drill sheets that coaches hand out at the range. AIcoach borrows that format: a stapled zine made by the club's coaching group, printed in fluorescent pink, teal and black on grey-blue duplicator stock. A zine is a modest object. Nobody expects one to be infallible, and that is why it suits a coach whose main selling point is honesty. Confidence isn't hidden in a tooltip. It's printed: a solid ink square means high, a half screen means medium, and a light dot screen means low. The same three densities appear on every measurement, chain link, library row and chat source. The golfer figures are halftone prints with misregistered plates. The result reads like a spread about your swing, and the drill and mobility exercise are cut-out cards you can take to the range. The chat is the zine's letters page, but you still type into it and get an answer.

Palette

HexRole
#E3E8EAPaper: grey-blue duplicator stock, the page ground (deliberately not cream)
#FBFBF7Card stock: spreads, cut-out cards, inputs
#FF48B0Fluorescent pink ink: the fault plate, primary buttons, backside line at address, highlighter fields (only behind black text, never as text)
#00838ATeal ink: the body plate, headline key plate, confidence swatches, step numerals (large sizes only)
#13285ENavy: the overprint, where pink and teal overlap. Verified stamps, measurements ("7%"), links, feel cue
#1D1B20Riso black: body text, body lines on key frames, club, destructive buttons
#F7C6E1Pink at about 30%: feel cue strip, current analysing pass, letters from the player

Typography

  • Dela Gothic One 400: headlines, verdicts, stamps, step numerals, "3 × 10 reps". A heavy, wide Japanese-poster gothic that keeps its shape when overprinted with a misregistered second plate. Headlines are set in sentence case and never tracked out.
  • Zilla Slab 400/500/600/700 + italic: all reading text, UI, labels and chat. Its slab serifs look like a typewritten handout. Italic carries the feel cue, captions and the player's letters.
  • Scale: 88 / 58 / 40 / 34 / 24 display; 25 / 22 / 18 / 17 / 15 / 13 text. Body is 17–18 px with a 1.5 line height and lines under 75 characters.

Signature moves

1. Confidence printed as ink coverage. Solid ink means high, a 50% halftone screen means medium and a 15% screen means low, and the band word is always printed beside the swatch. The landing explains it once ("Confidence is printed as ink"). After that it reads without a legend. 2. True overprint, real misregistration. Every headline and figure is printed as two plates: pink offset by a few pixels, teal on top, and navy wherever they overlap (computed with SVG masks, not faked with opacity). Golfer figures are halftone dot screens (SVG patterns at riso screen angles: 15° teal, 75° pink) over a flat pink plate. Ink speckle drops out of solid areas. 3. Stapled-page rhythm. Landing and result are a sequence of two-page spreads with a fold, two staples and page numbers. The result is a four-page issue about your swing: verdict + key frames, then fault chain + explanation. 4. Cut-out practice cards. Wall drill and 90/90 hip rotation are cards with dashed cut lines and scissors, each with its own halftone illustration (wall at the backside line, seated 90/90). The mobility card carries "Generic guidance, not medical advice — see a physiotherapist if you feel pain".

How the AI chat lives here

The chat is "Letters to the coach", the last page of the result issue. Rory's question is set as a pink-tint letter. The coach's reply is typeset on stock with a "Based on" row of source chips (7% of body height · Impact key frame · Wall drill), and each chip carries its confidence ink. A drawn page icon sits next to the grounding note: "Answers are based only on this analysis. The coach will not add faults, numbers or drills." Suggested prompts are tear-off tabs, like a noticeboard flyer, and tapping one sends it. The input is a real single-line field with a caret and a pink "Send" button. A note explains that off-topic questions get "cannot answer from your swing". On mobile the chat docks as a bar at the bottom of the result screen. The verdict spread links down to it with "Write to the coach at the end of this issue".

Risks / trade-offs

  • Charm vs. seriousness. Fluorescent pink and stamps could read as playful to a +2 player. The coaching content stays plain and exact, and the bold ink is kept for structure, but a more conservative audience may want a quieter variant (e.g. teal + black only).
  • Halftone costs legibility. Dot screens under text would hurt readability, so text never sits on a screen; it sits on card stock or flat tint. In code, the halftone patterns and overprint masks need care to stay sharp and fast on low-end phones. Rendering them as pre-built SVG/PNG assets is likely.
  • Spreads vs. scrolling. The fold-and-staple rhythm is a desktop conceit. On a phone it collapses into single pages, and the zine identity there rests mostly on the inks, stamps and cards.

---

Design plan (pass 1)

Tokens

  • Colour: paper #E3E8EA, card #FBFBF7, pink #FF48B0, teal #00838A, overprint navy #13285E, riso black #1D1B20.
  • Type: Dela Gothic One (display, overprinted), Zilla Slab (text/UI).
  • Layout: two-page spreads (1312 wide, fold at centre, staples at ¼ and ¾ height). Left page carries words or the verdict, right page carries the picture or evidence. Everything is left-aligned; centred text appears only inside stamps and buttons. Pasted items (photos, notices, cards) rotate up to ±1.6° as paste-up evidence. Data (rulers, chain, tables) is never rotated.
  • Principles: (1) ink density = certainty, nowhere else; (2) one boldness spent: the overprint; everything else is quiet slab text on stock; (3) numbers only where the content really is a sequence (how-it-works steps, filming-guide steps that rejections link to, analysing passes, drill steps); (4) no text on halftone.

Landing wireframe ` [AIcoach~] a practice zine… How it works Example Honesty Sign in [Create account] ============================================================================================= FILM ONE | ┌───────── pasted halftone print ──────────┐ SWING. | │ 7% box ← ┆ │ golfer (pink+teal plates) │ [Verified stamp] GET ONE | │ ┆ │ │ HONEST FIX. | │ caption: impact frame, synthetic data │ sub (3 lines) | └───────────────────────────────────────────┘ [Create account] [See an example result] -------------------------------- Issue 1 ---------------------- Example data is synthetic -- ┌──── page 2 ───────────────┬──── page 3 ────────────────────┐ │ How it works 1 2 3 ║ Where to put the phone: ticks │ (top-down DTL diagram) └───────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘ ┌──── page 4: key frames ───┬──── page 5: verdict, ruler, chain, feel cue ┐ ┌──── page 6: honesty + ink legend ║ page 7: pasted notices (reject / no fault / possible) ┐ Three faults table (fault · measure · cause · drill · mobility) Back cover: "Bring one swing." [Create account] colophon `

Result wireframe ` issue strip: date, club, fps [ ] Save to swing library Delete analysis ┌ p1: EARLY / EXTENSION, stamps, statement, 0–10% ruler, feel cue strip ┃ p2: address | impact key frames ┐ ┌ p3: fault chain (cause→mechanism→fault, hip-turn diagram) ┃ p4: explanation, also checked ┐ Take these to the range: [✂ Wall drill card] [✂ 90/90 card + medical disclaimer] Letters to the coach: letter / reply + "Based on" chips / input [Send] | tear-off prompts `

Plan review (what changed from the first instinct, and why)

  • Paper: my first instinct was cream newsprint with red + blue riso. Nine of the ten existing concepts already sit on cream or warm off-white, and #10 owns blue + red. I switched to grey-blue duplicator stock with fluorescent pink + teal, which has its own overprint colour (navy) to use for meaning.
  • Hero: I first sketched the feel-vs-real as an address/impact silhouette overlay. #10 (Kinetic Poster) already does ghost-vs-solid overlay, so I dropped it. The overlay is now only a riso texture (plate misregistration on one pose), and the address/impact comparison is shown as two side-by-side key frames with body lines, which is also closer to the PRD's "key frame".
  • Big-number hero: the "7%" started as a giant stat. That is the hero-metric template, so 7% now lives on a ruler against the 4% threshold and in a small callout on the print.
  • Display face: my first pick was a round fat face (Bagel-style), but it felt too cute for adult club golfers. Dela Gothic One is just as heavy but more poster than toy.
  • Confidence encoding: colour-coded chips (green/amber/red) were the default. I replaced them with ink coverage, which belongs to this world and doesn't depend on hue (it also works for colour-blind readers and in black-and-white print).
  • Progress vs. confidence: analysing passes first reused the density squares. I changed them to filled/partial/dashed circles so ink density means only certainty.
  • Rejected along the way: all-caps labels, eyebrows above headings, middle-dot meta strings, arrows appended to buttons, and text set on halftone.

Self-critique notes (after rendering)

  • Fixed: key frames overflowed their panels, the chat reply collided with the input, notice text overlapped a stamp, and back-cover copy sat on dots (it now sits on card inside a halftone frame).
  • Still a stretch: the seated 90/90 figure is schematic. A real build would commission proper halftone illustrations per drill. The first result spread has some empty space under the feel cue, which could take the hip-turn diagram on mobile.
12

Wayfinding Pictogram

Your swing, signposted: one pictogram per concept, one meaning per colour, and every arrow leads to what to practise.

Concept notes

Thesis: AIcoach treats your result like the signs in a good sports venue. Every concept has its own pictogram, every colour means exactly one thing, and every arrow takes you somewhere.

Rationale

This is for the 2–15 handicap player standing at the range with a phone in one hand and a club in the other. They have about two seconds of attention and maybe glare on the screen. Wayfinding signage is built for exactly that: people moving, glancing, under stress, who need the right answer fast. Signage also fits an honest coach, because a sign system only works if its codes are strict. Slate always means "verified by the rule table" and yellow always means "possible or unverified", so the app cannot dress up a guess as a fact without breaking its own rules. The fault chain becomes a signposted route (likely cause, then mechanism, then fault) that runs straight into the green "what to practise" exit. The filming guide is a set of pictogram plates you can read at arm's length. "Cannot analyse" is a stop sign whose reasons point to the filming-guide step that fixes each one.

Design plan (pass 1)

  • Colour, as sign enamel with strict meaning: slate #22313F = verified; signal yellow #F2C230 = possible / unverified / likely cause (not measured directly); green #0B7A53 = your next move (drills, exercises, primary actions); blue #1F5FAD = information desk (AI coach, filming guide); red #C8312A = stop (cannot analyse, delete). Neutral structure: concourse grey #E4E7E5 walls, white #FFFFFF sign blanks, metal #8C979D hanging rods.
  • Type: Overpass (its letterforms come from US highway-sign lettering) at 700–800 for every sign face. Atkinson Hyperlegible for body text, chat and small print. It was drawn for low-vision legibility and has distinct 0/O and I/l/1.
  • Layout: a modular sign system. Panels bolt together with 6 px gaps, each row is one fact, and the pictogram plate always sits at the left. Everything is left-aligned, as in directional signage. Station labels on route lines are centred under their stations, the only centred text.
  • Pictograms: an original family on a 100-unit grid with 8-unit round strokes and a detached disc head. The golfer is always in down-the-line profile, which matches the camera view. The plate always inverts the panel colour.
  • Principles: one meaning per colour; arrows only where they navigate; a pictogram for every concept; nothing shown without its confidence band.

` LANDING RESULT [logo] links ............ [Create] [logo] ........ Upload Library Guide (Rory) || || < Swing library Result: 7-iron [o] Save Film one swing. ================== +--------------------------+ +-----------+ Get directions, | Example result | |[PICT] Verified fault | | (i) INFO | not guesses. |##[pict] Early ext| | EARLY EXTENSION conf ■■■| | DESK | body copy |%%[pict] Posture | +--------------------------+ | grounded | [Create][Guide] | [pict] OTT n/f | [Address frame][Impact frame] | chat ... | |>>[pict] Practise->| [feel......][....real slate] | chips | (1)---->(2)---->(3) how it works What's happening (text) [ask->]| [input >] | [frames][scale/feel] [yellow]->[slate]->[slate] +-----------+ [yel]->[slate]->[slate]->[green] | | On this | legend | stop / no fault / unverified [green drill][green mobility] | page <- | 3 faults ... [ green exit sign ---> ] [yellow possible][white n/f] +-----------+ `

Plan review (what I changed from my first instinct, and why)

  • First instinct: airport black with yellow text, all caps. That is the "near-black with one bright accent" default, it reads like a real airport's trade dress, and all-caps labels are a known tell. Changed to a light concourse-grey world with five colours that each carry one meaning, set in sentence case. Mixed case is also more legible at a glance, which is the reason signage exists.
  • First instinct: a Helvetica-style neutral grotesk. That would fall back to the platform look. Changed to Overpass, a typeface with road-sign lineage, paired with Atkinson Hyperlegible for body text. The pairing is chosen for legibility rather than being the usual safe pick.
  • First instinct: the result as a grid of rounded cards with icons (the SaaS kit). Changed to a hanging directory board of bolted-together sign rows. Each row is one finding, and its colour tells you its status before you read it.
  • First instinct: green for "good / no fault" and red for "fault". That would turn the result into a pass/fail traffic light and moralise the swing. Changed: a verified fault is slate, which reads as a calm fact. Green is reserved for "your next move", so the route always ends at a green sign.
  • First instinct: a floating chat bubble in the corner. Changed to a docked Information desk with its own pictogram (a person behind a counter). It is blue because blue means information everywhere in the system.
  • Cut: a "you are here" dot on the hero and a progress percentage on the analysing screen. The analysing screen is a route line with stations instead, because it is a real sequence.

Palette

HexRole
#E4E7E5Concourse wall: page background
#FFFFFFSign blank: neutral panels, inputs, "not found" / "no verified fault" signs
#22313FSlate: verified (rule-table facts, measured mechanism) and all text and arrows
#F2C230Signal yellow: possible fault, unverified observation, likely cause (not directly measured)
#0B7A53Green: your next move (drill, mobility exercise, primary buttons)
#1F5FADBlue: information desk (AI coach chat, filming guide, help links)
#C8312ARed: stop (cannot analyse, delete analysis or account)
#55636ESecondary text (meta, captions)
#8C979DMetal: hanging-sign rods only
#8DA3AE / #5F7A5C / #3E4C44Key-frame scene (sky, turf, mat), flat and behind the figure

Typography

  • Overpass 700/800: sign faces, headings, buttons, route station names, numbers on signs. Tracking is tightened slightly (-0.02 em) at display sizes.
  • Atkinson Hyperlegible 400/700: body text, coach explanation, chat, consent and disclaimer text. The slashed zero helps make "0:06" and "120 fps" unambiguous.

Signature moves

1. Original pictogram family. Golfer at address, at impact, hips moving forward (with the dashed address line), wall drill, 90/90 stretch, phone on tripod, DTL plan view, hand height, distance, whole body in frame, one swing per clip, face-on, feet out of frame, 30 vs 120 fps, cannot analyse, information desk, likely-cause/unverified "?" and more. All share one stroke and grid, and the plate always inverts the panel colour. 2. Colour as law. Slate means verified, yellow possible/unverified, green next move, blue information, red stop. The landing page prints this legend, and every screen obeys it, down to the swing-library chips. 3. The fault chain as a signposted route (yellow likely cause, then slate mechanism, then slate fault). A thick route arrow drops straight into the green practise signs. 4. The split feel-cue sign. "It may feel like you stay down," sits on a white blank and "but at impact your hips have moved toward the ball." on slate, so the perceived and the verified are literally two different sign colours. 5. The analysing screen as a route line with five stations (pose, swing events, measurements, rule table, explanation). Done, current and waiting stations look different.

How the AI chat lives here

The chat is the Information desk, a docked blue-headed panel beside the result with a person-behind-a-counter pictogram. Directly under the header, a blue strip with a lock pictogram says: "Answers are based only on this analysis. No new faults, numbers or drills." Each coach answer ends with Based on tags that name the evidence it used ("Hips moved 7%", "Impact key frame", "Wall drill"). Suggested questions are outlined blue chips. The "What's happening" text has a blue pointer sign whose arrow aims at the desk. On mobile the desk becomes a blue bar at the bottom of the screen. On Nelly's no-fault result it offers to explain what "unverified" means.

Risks / trade-offs

  • Pictograms need learning. A plan-view "down the line" glyph or a 90/90 stretch is not instantly readable, so every pictogram ships with a text label. The system would need user testing at the range before any glyph is allowed to stand alone.
  • Key frames drawn as pictograms. In this sketch the key frames are rendered in the pictogram language. The real product shows video stills with body lines drawn over them, which will look busier than the signs around them. The overlay style (white dashed address line, slate impact line, joint dots) is designed to carry over.
  • Strict colour codes constrain branding. Green cannot become a "success" colour and red cannot mark a fault, so marketing and states have fewer options. Anyone extending the system has to respect the legend, or the honesty argument falls apart.
13

Anatomy Atlas

Every swing fault starts somewhere in your body.

Concept notes

Thesis: The body is the subject. AIcoach draws your swing as an anatomical atlas plate and follows the fault back through your joints to where it starts.

Rationale

This is for the 2 to 15 handicap player who has been told "you stand up out of it" and never told why. An atlas plate is the most trusted way people have to show cause inside a body: a precise figure, a few lettered points and a thin leader line to each label. That form suits an honest coach. Every label sits next to the evidence it points at, and the leader line itself shows how sure the app is. The fault chain stops being a list and becomes a route through the body: the lead hip (A) turns too little, the pelvis (B) slides toward the ball, and the spine (C) rises. That is early extension. Because the cause sits in the body, the mobility exercise gets its own plate, the same size as the drill. The atlas is also strict about its limits: it says it shows the pose found in the video, and the page says plainly that this is coaching, not diagnosis.

Palette

HexRole
#E4E2DBBone: page ground (greyed, cooler than cream)
#EFEDE7Plate paper: inside atlas plate frames
#25323CSlate ink: text, outlines, buttons, leader lines
#53616CSecondary slate: captions, thresholds, muted text
#A9BCC6Tissue: the translucent body (outline #7C93A0)
#F7F3EABone fill: skeleton
#B0283CBodily red: only the joint in question and the cause route. Never a button or a heading
#34444FConsult slate: the AI coach chat panel

Typography (Google Fonts)

  • Atkinson Hyperlegible Next (400/700/800). It does all the UI, the headlines and every number. It was designed for legibility in low vision, which helps on a phone in bright sun at the range. It reads clinical without feeling cold. Headlines are 800 with slightly tight tracking.
  • Spectral italic (400/500). It is used only for atlas annotation: plate captions ("Plate 1. Impact, seen down the line"), chain roles ("Likely cause"), scale labels ("threshold 4%") and short marginal notes. It is never used for headlines.

Signature moves

1. The plate: the golfer is a translucent, side-on body outline over a simplified skeleton (pelvis, vertebrae, ribcage, femurs). The address pose stays faintly behind the impact pose. An "address line" with a red 7% dimension shows the hips moving toward the ball. 2. Confidence is the leader line: a solid leader means high, dashed means medium and dotted means low. The text "Confidence: …" always appears too. A "Key to the plates" legend on the landing page teaches this once. 3. The cause route: a red dotted route runs A → B → C through the body on the hero plate. On the result page, three plates (a pelvis seen from above with a 31° arc against ~45°, a close-up of the pelvis sliding forward, and the whole figure) are joined by red arrows. 4. Equal-weight practice plates: the wall drill is shown side-on with the wall hatched and the half-swing arc. The 90/90 hip rotation is shown from above with a rotation arc. They are the same size, and each says which link it works on ("Trains B", "Works on A").

How the AI chat lives here

The chat is a slate "consult" panel next to the plates. It can point at the body. When the coach mentions the pelvis, a chip ("Showing B on Plate 1: pelvis at impact") lines up with the B label, a line joins them, and the B label is highlighted. That ties every answer to a lettered point that is already evidenced. "Answers are based only on this analysis. No new faults, numbers or drills" sits under the title. The secondary sheet shows the coach declining to talk about grip, because it was not measured, and sending a pain question to a physiotherapist.

Risks and trade-offs

  • An anatomical skeleton can feel medical or a little morbid to some golfers. It also risks implying a diagnosis, so the "coaching, not diagnosis" line has to stay visible, and the figure has to stay schematic.
  • Drawing a figure from 2D pose estimates is an honest picture of the data, but a real build needs a solid way to fit the plate figure to the keypoints. If the fit is poor, the figure looks wrong on unusual body shapes.
  • The pages are long and dense with annotation (the landing page is about 4500 px). The atlas grammar rewards close reading, while players at the range only glance, so the phone result has to stay much more compressed.

Design plan (pass 1)

  • Color: bone ground, plate paper, slate ink, translucent tissue blue-grey, bone fill, one bodily red for the joint in question, a consult slate for the chat.
  • Type: a hyperlegible sans for everything people read and act on. A book italic only for the atlas's own annotations.
  • Layout: left-aligned, ragged-right text. The plates are the largest objects on every page. Each plate's labels sit in a margin column, joined to the body by elbowed leader lines. Desktop result:

` +-------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------+

AIcoach Upload Library Guide Acct
Early extension Verified fault --- Confidence: highASK THE COACH
+---------------------------------------------------------+(slate panel)
[key frame: address] [key frame: impact] (C) SpineRory: why...
figure+skeleton figure+ghost --- (A) Lead hipCoach: ...
address line 7% dim ------------ (B) Pelvis ==== [B chip]
scale 0..10% threshold 4 ^7% Plate 1 cap....
+---------------------------------------------------------+chips / input
How it happened: [A dial 31°] -> [B pelvis] -> [C figure]
Feel cue (italic, large)Explanation (coach voice)
[Plate 3 Wall drill] [Plate 4 90/90 from above]
Also checked: Loss of posture (possible), Over the top
Save to swing library

+-------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------+ `

  • Principles: prove it on the body, never in a stat tile. Leader-line style is data. Red appears only where the fault starts. Every number sits next to its threshold.

Plan review: what changed from first instinct

  • First instinct: Spectral serif headlines on a warm cream plate with an oxblood accent and hairline rules. That is the cream + serif + clay cliché, with the broadsheet hairlines on top. Changed: the ground moved to a greyer, cooler bone (#E4E2DB) and the chat went onto a cool slate. Headlines are now a heavy hyperlegible sans, and the serif is demoted to italic annotation only. Red is limited to anatomy, so CTAs are slate.
  • First instinct: coloured confidence pills (green, amber, grey). That is a generic dashboard habit, and it would compete with the red joint. Changed: confidence is encoded in the atlas's own device, the leader line (solid, dashed, dotted), and the word is always spelled out.
  • First instinct: 01 / 02 / 03 section numbers. Changed: letters A, B and C are used only for anatomical points in chain order, because the chat refers to them. Numerals appear only where there is a real sequence: the three "Film, upload, read" steps and the filming-guide steps that rejection reasons link to.
  • First instinct: a single big figure with a stat callout in the hero. Changed: the hero is a full plate with margin labels and a cause route. The 7% is shown as a dimension on the body, not as a big number.
  • First instinct: drawing the 90/90 exercise side-on like the drill. Changed: it is drawn from above, the same transverse view as the 31° hip dial, so the exercise visibly trains the same rotation the measurement found lacking.

Self-critique notes

  • Rendered every file in headless Chrome and fixed the following: overlapping header labels on the contact sheet, a "6°" label colliding with the skull, a rejection card that implied a confidence band, the gap in the chat thread, and text below 12 px inside scaled diagrams.
  • The figure geometry is generated from one set of joints (pose()), so address, impact and drills stay anatomically consistent across all files.
  • Known weak spot: the 90/90 top view is schematic, and some people may need its caption ("seen from above") to read it.
14

Pro Shop 1974

Your swing comes back as the pro's lesson card: warm, a bit old-fashioned, and it never bluffs.

Concept notes

Thesis: Your swing comes back as the pro's lesson card. It's warm and a bit old-fashioned, and it never bluffs.

Rationale

This is for the 11-handicapper who has not had a lesson in three years. He remembers the club pro's shop: a pennant wall, a counter, and a pro who wrote one thing on a card and sent you back to the mat. AIcoach keeps that ritual. The result is a printed lesson card with a sweater-stripe band across the top, and the drill and mobility exercise are illustrated lesson tiles like the ones in a 1970s instruction book. The warmth is there on purpose. A coach that often says "Cannot analyse", "No verified fault found" or "Unverified — confirm with a coach" needs a friendly voice, so that saying no feels like care and not like an error. The 1970s styling stays on the surface. Every honest element is drawn plainly and labelled in words: confidence bands, thresholds on a yardstick ruler, and evidence for each link of the chain.

Palette

HexNameRole
#3A2214ChocolateInk, corduroy nav, chat panel, primary buttons (mustard text), fault stripe
#E0A526MustardHero ground, rulers, CTA on dark, likely-cause stripe, done states
#C4551BBurnt orangeMechanism stripe, sweater stripes, cap. Used only for shapes and large text
#A3410FRustSmall accent text: links, thresholds, link-role labels (5.4:1 on card stock)
#66702AAvocado feltFelt panels (drop zone, drill tile, honesty band), Verified badge
#F4ECD6Card stockOnly the lesson card and slips. Never used as the page background
#DCD6B2PuttyApp page background (felt-dot texture)
#CFCB9CSageBackground of key-frame stills

Typography

  • Caprasimo (Google Fonts, 400): a fat soft serif with 1970s swagger. Used for headlines, fault names, the feel-cue quote and the "Ask the pro" title.
  • Libre Franklin (400–800, italic 400/500): a plain American grotesque. Used for all body text, labels, measurements and chat text. Labels are in sentence case and never tracked caps.

Signature moves

1. The stripes carry the fault chain. On the result page, a band of three sweater stripes (chocolate, orange, mustard) comes in from the edge of the card. Each stripe peels down in a rounded 70s bend into its own link card: mustard into the likely cause, orange into the mechanism, chocolate into the fault. The same three stripes are the brand band elsewhere, and on the analysing screen they act as the progress track. 2. The flat 1970s instruction-book golfer. He wears a mustard sweater with stripes, a flat cap and saddle shoes. He is drawn down the line, with body lines (white core, chocolate edge) and a dashed rust "address line" that shows how far the hips moved by impact. 3. Honest instruments in period dress. A wooden yardstick ruler marks the threshold and the measured value (7% against 4%). The confidence badge is a three-notch meter plus the word. Colour never carries the meaning alone. The pennant wall in the landing page's "pro shop" lists the three faults and how confident each can be. Over the top hangs there as "Capped at medium confidence".

How the AI chat lives here

The chat is "Ask the pro", a chocolate corduroy panel that stays beside the lesson card on desktop and becomes a floating "Ask the pro about this lesson" bar on the phone. Under the header it always says "Answers are based only on this analysis." Every answer from the pro carries mustard chips labelled "From this analysis:" (Impact key frame, 7% measurement, Wall drill), so the player can see what grounds each reply. The sample also shows a refusal: "Should I change my grip?" gets "I can't tell you that. This analysis didn't measure your grip, so I won't guess." The voice is a plain, warm club pro, not a chatbot.

Risks and trade-offs

  • Nostalgia can read as costume. Push it further, for example with an ochre wash on everything, and it turns into a theme-restaurant menu. It only holds if the stripes stay meaningful and the reading surfaces stay calm.
  • Caprasimo is greedy. It is wide and heavy, so long fault names wrap early on the phone. It needs strict size limits and a rule that it is never used for body text or small labels.
  • Orange has weak contrast. Burnt orange fails for small text on light grounds, so the system needs a separate rust for text. A developer could easily mix the two up.

Design plan (pass 1)

  • Colour: chocolate #3A2214, mustard #E0A526, burnt orange #C4551B, avocado #66702A, card stock #F4ECD6, putty #DCD6B2.
  • Type: Caprasimo for display, Libre Franklin for text.
  • Layout: Left-aligned throughout. Sections alternate grounds like the walls of a shop: mustard corduroy for the hero, chocolate corduroy for the pennant wall, putty felt for the steps, avocado felt for honesty. The result page is one long lesson card (880 wide) with "Ask the pro" pinned in a 400-wide column beside it.

` LANDING RESULT [corduroy nav ...........................] [corduroy nav ...........................] [Film one swing. | /lesson card\ ] [ LESSON CARD ==stripes== | ASK THE PRO ] [Get the lesson | | key frames | ] [ Early extension [V][hi] | Answers are..] [card back. [CTA] | | ruler 7% | ] [ [address] [impact] | Rory: why.. ] [==== mustard / orange / choc band =====] [ ruler ----4%-----7%---- | Pro: ... 6° ] [ pennant wall: 3 faults hanging ] [ ~~~ feel cue (mustard) ~~ | [chips] ] [ 1 ===== 2 ===== 3 how a lesson works ] [ What the pro says | [input] ] [ honesty: slip | Nelly | conf legend ] [ ==stripes peel into== | ] [ ask the pro: copy | chat ] [ [cause] > [mech] > [fault] ] [ close: Bring one swing to the counter ] [ [drill tile] [mobility tile] ] [ also checked / save / delete ] `

  • Principles: stripes carry meaning, not just decoration. Card stock appears only where something is "printed". Confidence is always written in words. One instruction-book illustrator draws every figure.

Plan review: what I changed from my first instinct

  • I dropped the cream page with a terracotta accent. My first instinct was a cream page with Cooper-style type and an orange accent, which is exactly cliché #1. Mustard corduroy and putty felt now carry the page. Card stock is kept for the lesson card itself, and orange is never the only accent.
  • Confidence is a notch meter, not a traffic light. Green, yellow and red would have competed with the stripe colours that encode the chain, and would have relied on colour alone. Confidence is now a one-ink, three-notch meter plus the word.
  • No vintage-manual tracked caps. Period instruction books lean on tracked uppercase labels, which is also cliché #5. All labels are sentence-case Libre Franklin bold.
  • The stripes were going to be pure decoration. I first drew them as the hero's racing stripes. I moved their meaning into the product: they show the order of the fault chain on the result page and the progress on the analysing screen. On the landing page they stay as one band between sections.
  • I avoided equal slanted bars. Three equal slanted stripes come too close to a famous sportswear trade dress. These stripes are horizontal, unequal in colour and bent in curves, and the logo is a pennant badge.
15

Pocket Device

Load one swing into a small, honest instrument: it answers on its display, and explains itself in the owner's manual.

Concept notes

Thesis: AIcoach is a small, well-made instrument you load one swing into. It answers on its own display, and the full explanation comes as printed pages from its owner's manual.

Rationale

This concept is for the 11-handicap who practises after work and trusts tools more than talk: a rangefinder, a good wedge, a launch monitor at the shop. Turning the coach into a piece of hardware makes the honesty physical. The device has a fixed set of display messages ("cannot analyse", "no verified fault", "unverified"), a confidence meter that always shows, and a clip slot that accepts exactly one swing. A device can only show what it measured, and that is the promise PRD §1 makes. The playful object (screws, knurled dial, speaker grille, a swing clip as a labelled cartridge) makes a strict tool feel friendly instead of clinical. The reading itself happens on paper: the explanation, fault chain and drills are set as owner's-manual pages in plain proportional type, so the result page still reads like a coach's note rather than a gadget readout.

Palette

HexRole
#E5E4EEStudio sweep: page background, the "product shot" backdrop
#A3A7D6Anodised periwinkle device body (gradient #B7BBE4 → #8E92C4, edge #7B7FB3)
#2B2D54Recess: display bezels, slot, grille holes, switch tracks
#1D1F3FInk: silkscreen and printed text (secondary #3A3D6B, #4A4D78)
#CDD3B6Reflective LCD (segment ink #262B1E, silhouette #8C9476, unlit segments #C7CDAF)
#F4C430Signal yellow: the one primary key per view ("Create account", "Choose clip", "analyse swing", "Load another clip"), the active stage LED, and the switch when it is on
#FBFBF8Manual paper (rules #D7D7E2)

Typography (Google Fonts)

  • Encode Sans Expanded 500–800: device silkscreen, headlines, keycap labels. A wide grotesk reads like printed panel lettering. Labels stay lowercase, as small silkscreen does, with no all-caps eyebrows.
